title: Origami: Folding Goodness
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss origami (Japanese paper folding), starting with a personal anecdote about Hiroshima and the thousand paper cranes associated with Sadako Sasaki, and a coworker's (Pam's) project folding a thousand cranes. They cover the etymology of origami (oru and kami), paper history from China to Japan, the rise of origami as an art form led by Akira Yoshizawa and his diagramming system and wet folding, basic bases (kite, fish, bird, frog), categories such as modular, action origami, tessellations, and pure land origami, types of paper (kami, washi, Japanese foil), technical versus free-form origami as shown in the documentary Between the Folds, and practical applications of origami-inspired folding. The episode ends with a listener mail about sneezing and arousal and a sign-off.

segments.title: Book plug and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts plug their upcoming book and open with banter about a trip to Japan, Hiroshima, and the thousand-crane tradition tied to Sadako Sasaki.

segments.title: Coworker's thousand-crane project and origami as meditation
segments.summary: Pam, a graphic designer at the hosts' company, folded a thousand cranes within a year, citing meditation, dexterity, and discipline. The hosts discuss origami as transformative and reference Between the Folds and Michael LaFosse's view of origami as metamorphic.

segments.title: Origami vs. bonsai and definitions
segments.summary: The hosts compare origami to bonsai, note that origami uses one sheet of paper without glue or cutting, and explain the etymology of origami from oru (to fold) and kami (paper).

segments.title: Origami supplies and terminology
segments.summary: Origami needs only paper; finished works are called models. Step-by-step diagrams make imagination unnecessary. British John Smith's pure land origami was designed for people with physical impairments.

segments.title: Non-origami banter and break
segments.summary: Hosts chat about a Christopher Nolan film, movie theaters, and a comedian joke before a break; no ad read in this section.

segments.title: History of paper and origami in China and Japan
segments.summary: Paper was invented in China around 105 AD and was luxurious; Buddhist monks introduced paper to Japan in the sixth century. Folding spread as paper became affordable, with forms like shide and cranes; an eighteenth-century book on folding a thousand cranes is cited.

segments.title: Akira Yoshizawa and origami as art
segments.summary: Akira Yoshizawa turned origami from a children's craft into an art form in the 1930s, published diagramming in the 1950s, popularized wet folding, made many models, never sold them, and supported himself selling soup door to door.

segments.title: Basic origami techniques and bases
segments.summary: Hosts describe the kite, fish, bird, and frog bases, the paperkawaii resource with twelve bases, and that models are held together by folds rather than glue or tape. Tips include using a desk, clipboard, or paper clips for creases.

segments.title: Origami categories and paper types
segments.summary: Categories include modular, action origami, origami fortune tellers, tessellations, and origami from dollar bills, sticky notes, and jewelry. Paper types discussed include kami, washi for wet folding, and Japanese foil.

segments.title: Listener mail on sneezing and arousal
segments.summary: A listener named Darcy wrote in about a link between arousal and a running nose after the sneezing episode. The hosts read it and sign off.
